# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical reading of Lindqvist, Mahony, Rao & Okafor, "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This is the strongest document so far. It directly addresses several gaps raised about the earlier papers:

- **Unrecorded work.** It adds system-log hours alongside timesheets.
- **Meeting baseline.** It reports meeting time at baseline (7.4 hours in treated offices, 7.2 in control), which the nine-month report lacked.
- **Mechanism.** It registers a mediation test before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- **Counter-office comparison.** It reports counter-office waiting times against control offices, not just before and after.
- **Survivorship.** It clearly labels the Halden subset as survivors.
- **Durability.** It tests decay within the same study over time, instead of comparing different studies.

Its two rebuttals are largely sound. Varden now meets the standards Varga & Holm themselves set and still finds a gain. The four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis turn out to be uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours, which is exactly the concern I raised about the duration analysis.

There are still problems. Some come from presentation, one from a contaminated control group, and one from the main measure being ambiguous.

## What checks out

The headline arithmetic is correct:

| Figure | Calculation | Result | Reported |
|---|---|---|---|
| Varden, per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | 1.098 | +9.8% |
| Varden, per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | 1.085 | +8.5% |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | 0.866 | −13.4% |
| Halden continuers, per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 | 1.118 | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47% + 18% + 35% | 100% | 100% |

## Main problems

### 1. The summary overstates the decline

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". Those two figures use different hours measures: 12.5% is based on timesheets and 8.5% on system logs.

On the same measure, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%. That is a decline of about 22%, which the body correctly calls "about a quarter". Mixing the two measures makes the decline look like about a third. This changes the headline, so it should be corrected.

### 2. The control group was contaminated, which affects the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit" on their own initiative. Their output per hour then rose about 4% above their own previous six months.

The authors treat this only as a hint that the gain might be available without cutting hours. It also biases the main result. A difference-in-differences estimate compares treated offices with control offices. If control offices improve, the measured gap shrinks even when treated offices are unchanged. Some of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore reflect improvement in control offices, not fading in treated ones. Control staff probably knew the nine-month findings, since that report was published, so this is plausibly spillover.

The authors should report a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or truncated at month 15, together with a breakdown of how treated and control offices each moved. Until then, the size of the decay is uncertain in an unknown direction.

### 3. It is unclear what the system-log hours measure

The log measure is described as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases". Taken literally, that is case-work time, and meetings would not be logged. The numbers don't fit that reading, using the timesheet figures:

| | Before | At 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Hours worked | about 37.9 | about 33.4 (−12%) |
| Recurring meetings | 7.4 | 3.9 |
| Non-meeting time | about 30.5 | about 29.5 |

Non-meeting time fell only about 3%. If the logs captured case-work time alone, they should show a fall of a few percent, not the 11% reported. So either the logs include meeting time (for instance, staff stay logged in during meetings), or something else is going on.

This matters for interpreting the mediation result:

- **If logs include meeting time:** the meetings pathway is largely mechanical. Hours spent in meetings are removed from the denominator with no loss of output. That is a real and useful gain, but it means less non-productive time, not faster work.
- **If logs are case-work time only:** fewer meetings would have to raise output per case-work hour through some other route, such as fewer interruptions or less task-switching. That is a different and more surprising claim.

The paper should say what the log measure covers and report its levels, not only percentage changes.

### 4. The mediation analysis is weaker than "confirms" suggests

The registration timing is genuine. It was filed at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes. Some caveats remain:

- **Same sample.** The hypothesis came from these same seven offices, and meeting data up to month 11 had already been seen. This is a confirmatory test in time, not an independent replication, so it only partly answers Varga & Holm's "does not replicate" concern.
- **Effective sample size.** The paper cites "a larger sample of office-months". Office-months within the same 14 offices are not independent observations. The effective sample is still 14 clusters, and the confidence intervals should reflect that.
- **Unstable shares.** Mediation shares of a small, imprecise total effect (8.5%, CI 3.4 to 13.8) tend to be unstable. The interval of 28% to 66% probably understates the uncertainty.
- **Confounding and timing.** The assumption of no mediator-outcome confounding is acknowledged. It is a strong assumption when managers who cut meetings may also have changed other practices. The timing of mediator and outcome measurement is also not described.

A fair summary would be: "a pre-registered test in the original sample supports a substantial role for meetings." "Confirms" overstates it.

### 5. Earlier gaps in case-processing remain

The nine-month report left several questions open that this follow-up does not answer:

- **Backlog and timeliness.** Queue length, time to decision and breaches of statutory deadlines are still not reported, even though the nine-month limitations raised backlog build-up.
- **Cost.** There is still no cost per case. Treated staff appear to work about 3 hours a week above their 30 scheduled hours, so overtime pay may be partly sustaining output.
- **Precision of quality and retention figures.** The appeal overturn rate (3.2% vs 3.0%) and resignations are still given without confidence intervals.

Output per employee is now −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2). The hours cut is mostly but not fully offset, and the authors say so. Without cost and backlog data, though, an employer still cannot judge whether the scheme pays for itself.

### 6. The Halden subset

The authors are appropriately cautious, calling these organisations "survivors twice over". A few further issues:

- **Baseline hours.** The 40.3-hour baseline is exactly the average for all 27 organisations with time tracking. The 11 continuing organisations need their own baseline.
- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. Those that didn't may well have reverted, so the count of three reversions out of 14 likely understates the true rate.
- **Long gap with no comparison group.** Output at 24 months is compared with a baseline about 2.5 years earlier and no comparison group. Over 2023–2025, changes such as new software tools and AI assistance could raise output per hour on their own. That alone makes "upper bound" uncertain.
- **Work-type coding.** One reverting organisation was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which is discretionary work by the meta-analysis's coding. Client-facing deadlines can create coverage-like constraints, so the discretionary/coverage-bound split is coarser than the meta-analysis implies.

### 7. Smaller points

- **Counter-office costs.** Closing the counter arm at month 12 is now backed by a proper controlled comparison (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes). That is a clear improvement. The 12% staffing increase and 9% cost increase are county estimates, not measured outcomes. They imply staff are about three-quarters of cost per contact, which is plausible but not stated.
- **The response to the energy extrapolation.** The rebuttal is fair: the gain clearly did not reach zero by month ten. Varga & Holm extrapolated self-reported energy, though, not output. The stronger point, which I made earlier, is that energy was never a good proxy for output.
- **Authorship.** The authors are rebutting criticism of their own earlier work. One of them, Okafor, wrote the original Halden paper. That doesn't invalidate anything, especially given the registered protocol. It does make independent replication, and release of the Varden data, particularly valuable.

## Where the evidence now stands

Across all five documents:

- **Output per hour.** In discretionary work, measured as rigorously as anyone has, the gain is roughly 8.5–10% at two years. It has declined somewhat from nine months, by an amount uncertain because of the control contamination. It has not disappeared. "Entirely an artifact" is not supported.
- **Output per employee.** In discretionary work, it is slightly below control (about −3%, CI includes zero). The hours cut is mostly but not fully offset, and cost per unit of output is still unreported.
- **Coverage-bound work.** Output and service fall, and maintaining service costs roughly 9% more per contact. The randomised arm was ended for this reason.
- **Mechanism.** Removing low-value meeting time looks like the largest identifiable component, about half, with fatigue a smaller contributor. This rests on one employer, 14 offices and an ambiguous hours measure.
- **The key open question.** Can reorganisation alone, such as a meeting audit without cutting hours, capture most of the gain? Or is the hours cut what forces reorganisation and makes it stick? The two control offices hint at the first but cannot settle it. A trial with a "reorganise only" arm is the obvious next study, and it would matter more to employers than another reduced-hours pilot.

Before relying on these 24-month figures, I would want four things from the authors:

1. a corrected summary using like-for-like figures;
2. a sensitivity analysis excluding the two contaminated control offices;
3. a definition of the log-hours measure, with levels;
4. backlog and cost data for case-processing offices.
